title: Your LLM Ran Out of Knowledge — Now What?

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on designing structured prompts with domain-specific heuristics and rules to program LLM reasoning in low-knowledge domains. The framework is explicitly domain-agnostic but demonstrated in corporate negotiations and geopolitics intelligence estimation. OracReasoningEngine is a working prototype with initial positive results that is still being refined. Requires prompt engineering and heuristic design knowledge but remains accessible to AI practitioners without deep ML expertise. The video combines conceptual explanation with a live walkthrough of the OracReasoningEngine processing geopolitics and negotiation scenarios. Seven transcript-grade evidence anchors directly support heuristics-based prompt design and the parsing engine as the primary subject.

The framework is explicitly domain-agnostic but demonstrated in corporate negotiations and geopolitics intelligence estimation. OracReasoningEngine is a working prototype with initial positive results that is still being refined. summary: The video explores a fundamental limitation of LLMs: they excel in domains with abundant structured training data like coding, math, and physics, but struggle in fields such as corporate negotiations, geopolitics, and risk management where expertise is tacit—held in practitioners' minds and never documented. The presenter, from a risk and security management background, acknowledges this gap stems from practitioners not writing things down, not from model trainers' shortcomings. The proposed solution mirrors a familiar workplace practice: organizations give intelligent but inexperienced recent graduates heuristics and rules of thumb to apply their intelligence in unfamiliar domains while building experience. Similarly, the framework provides LLMs with explicit domain-specific rules layered atop their reasoning capabilities. The demonstration walks through OracReasoningEngine, which processes user prompts in stages. First, a dedicated LLM matches the input against available heuristics—an approach chosen over standard tool use for greater granularity. Second, it standardizes the scenario into a consistent format. Third, it retrieves appropriate rule sets written in binary, provable terms (must do, must not do) from domain collections covering corporate negotiations and geopolitical strategy. Finally, it sends the structured prompt to a reasoning model—in this case, Anthropic's model paired with a world simulation that adds realistic geopolitical constraints including the UN, WTO, and physical geography. Results show the model following the prescribed structure, referencing specific rules like two times leverage and greater than 50% control, and eliminating scenarios that breach rules. The presenter emphasizes keeping human subject matter experts in the loop while leveraging the system's speed to generate and review dozens of scenarios rapidly. In closing, the presenter expresses hope that this technique will help others encountering similar low-knowledge domains, encouraging use of the parsing engine and rules of thumb in problem solving alongside LLMs to move models into currently underexplored areas.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Knowledge Gap Problem in Low-Data Domains
sections.summary: LLMs perform well in domains with structured training data like coding and math, but struggle in fields such as corporate negotiations, geopolitics, and risk management where knowledge is tacit and never written down. The presenter attributes this gap to practitioners not documenting their expertise, creating domains that are effectively left behind by advancing models.

sections.title: Heuristics as a Bridge for Domain Expertise
sections.summary: The proposed solution mirrors how organizations give intelligent but inexperienced recent graduates rules of thumb and heuristics to work in unfamiliar domains. The framework applies the same principle to LLMs: providing explicit domain-specific rules layered atop powerful reasoning capabilities to overcome wisdom gaps and enable work in specialized fields.

sections.title: Framework Walkthrough: Matching and Standardization
sections.summary: The demo shows OracReasoningEngine processing a geopolitics intelligence estimate prompt. The system first matches the input against available heuristics using a dedicated LLM (an alternative to tool use chosen for better granularity), then standardizes the scenario into a consistent structured format before sending it to the reasoning model.

sections.title: Rule Sets, World Simulation, and Model Selection
sections.summary: Rule sets for negotiations and geopolitics are written in binary, provable terms. A higher-level heuristics prompt governs behavior and pulls in the appropriate domain rules. The system sends structured prompts to a chosen reasoning model—Anthropic in this demo—paired with a world simulation adding realistic geopolitical constraints like the UN, WTO, and physical geography.

sections.title: Results and Reflections
sections.summary: Results show the model following the prescribed structure and referencing specific rules such as two times leverage and greater than 50% control, eliminating scenarios that breach rules. The presenter notes the approach enables rapid generation of dozens of scenarios for expert review, always keeping a human subject matter expert in the loop. Initial results are positive though the approach is still being refined.

sections.title: Closing: Extending the Technique to Underexplored Domains
sections.summary: The presenter closes by expressing hope that this technique—using the parsing engine, rules of thumb, and LLMs together—will help others who encounter similar low-knowledge domains, enabling problem-solving and potentially uncovering new approaches, ultimately moving models into areas that are currently underexplored.
